title: Reasoning via Prompting
oneLiner: Models solve hard problems better when they show their working, explore alternatives, use tools and check results, and they get better still when given more time to think.

what.html:
A model does a fixed amount of thinking per word it writes. So for multi-step problems, it helps to make it write the steps: chain-of-thought. Beyond a single chain, it can explore several paths (Tree of Thought), recall the principle first (step-back), write code to do the maths (PAL), use tools between thoughts (ReAct), learn from failed attempts (self-reflection), and simply try many times and pick the best (test-time compute).

Everyday versionA student solving an exam problem: writing out steps, sketching a few approaches, recalling the formula, using a calculator, checking the answer and fixing a mistake. Each habit makes the final answer more likely to be right.

why.html:
• These techniques turn the same model into a much better problem solver.
  • Modern "reasoning" models are built on these ideas.
  • ReAct is the heartbeat of AI agents.

how.title: Why steps help
how.html: Each written step gives the model more room to compute, and mistakes in hidden steps pile up. Writing steps makes them checkable too.

how.title: Show your working
how.html: "Let's think step by step." For 3 boxes of 12 eggs with 20 used: 3 × 12 = 36, then 36 − 20 = 16.

how.title: Explore a tree of ideas
how.html: Try several next steps, judge which look promising, and back up from dead ends, like solving a puzzle by trying moves.

how.title: Principle first, or write code
how.html: Step-back asks "which rule applies?" before answering. PAL lets the model write a tiny program and a computer does the arithmetic exactly.

how.title: Think, act, observe
how.html: Alternate thinking with tool use: look up the Eiffel Tower (330 m) and Qutub Minar (73 m), then subtract: 257 m.

how.title: Learn from mistakes
how.html: Try, run the tests, write down what went wrong, try again. Works best when there's a real check, like tests.

how.title: More thinking time
how.html: Ask many times and vote, or let a checker pick the best attempt. Answers 42, 42, 7, 42 → 42. More attempts cost more.

demo.html: Match each description to the reasoning technique.

example.html:
Game of 24. Numbers 4, 7, 8, 8. Starting with 8 × 8 = 64 leads nowhere; backing up and trying 4 + 7 = 11, then 11 − 8 = 3, then 8 × 3 = 24 works. That backing-up is what a tree search adds.

Supplementary A neat-looking chain of reasoning isn't proof the model actually reasoned that way, so check the answer, not just the explanation.

misunderstandings: Mostly for multi-step tasks and larger models.
The written reasoning is exactly how the model thought.
It works best with external checks.
takeaways: Fixed compute per token → write steps for multi-step problems.
CoT: few-shot or "think step by step" (3 × 12 − 20 = 16).
Step-back recalls principles; PAL computes with code; ReAct uses tools.
Self-reflection needs real feedback; test-time compute scales with samples and verifiers.
thirty: Models spend fixed computation per token, so multi-step problems benefit from explicit intermediate reasoning. Chain-of-thought elicits steps (few-shot examples or 'Let's think step by step'): 3 × 12 = 36, 36 − 20 = 16. Tree of Thought proposes candidate thoughts, evaluates states, and searches with pruning and backtracking (Game of 24: (4 + 7 − 8) × 8). Step-back prompting retrieves the governing principle first (PV = nRT → 4×); PAL writes code executed by an interpreter. ReAct interleaves Thought, Action and Observation (330 − 73 = 257 m), grounding answers in tool results. Self-reflection retries using written lessons from feedback (unit tests), and is unreliable without external signals. Test-time compute spends more inference: self-consistency voting (42, 42, 7, 42 → 42), best-of-n with verifiers, and long reasoning chains learned with RL.

check.q: Tree of Thought differs from CoT by…
opts: Exploring and backtracking over several paths
